div.p: Objective The C-PLAN index, which comprehensively considers inflammation, nutritional status, tumor grade/ metabolism, and functional status, has been proven to be an effective predictor of various cancers. However, its application in patients with high-grade glioma (HGG) has not been studied. Therefore, this study aimed to analyze the impact of the C-PLAN index on the survival of HGG patients.

div.head: Methods
div.p: This study included 140 HGG patients who underwent postoperative radiotherapy/radiochemotherapy between April 2011 and May 2024. Patient medical records were retrospectively analyzed. Demographic and clinical data (IDH status, surgical procedure, histopathological type, Karnofsky Performance Status) were analyzed. Overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were evaluated using Kaplan-Meier survival curves and Cox regression analysis.

div.head: Results
div.p: Data from 140 HGG patients were analyzed. The median survival was 12 months (IQR 25-75: 7-21 months). In univariate analysis, IDH status (χ 2 (1) = 11.17, p < 0.001), KPS score (χ 2 (1) = 29.57, p < 0.001), and C-PLAN index (χ 2 (1) = 8.83, p = 0.003) were significant predictors of OS. In the multivariate analysis, IDH status (p = 0.003, HR = 3.23 [95% CI: 1.47-7.09]) and KPS score (p < 0.001, HR = 2.68 [95% CI: 1.58-4.52]) remained significant predictors of OS, whereas the C-PLAN index was not significant (p = 0.17, HR = 0.69 [95% CI: 0.404-1.18]).

Discussion This is the first study to investigate the impact of the C-PLAN index on overall OS in patients with HGG. The results showed that in univariate analysis, IDH status, Karnofsky Functional Status Score (KPS), and the C-PLAN index were significant predictors of OS in HGG patients. In multivariate analysis, all factors except the C-PLAN index were also significant. Further research is needed to confirm these findings.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: e most deadly and aggressive primary brain tumors in adults are high-grade gliomas (HGGs), which include glioblastoma (GBM). e median overall survival (OS) is lower than 15 months despite advances in surgical resection, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy [1]. e heterogeneity of these tumors at both the molecular and clinical levels has prompted the search for prognostic biomarkers to more precisely stratify patients and develop individualized treatment plans.

e prognostic significance of several factors has been established, such as the extent of surgical resection, patient age and general condition at diagnosis, and the histopathological characteristics of the tumor (e.g., the state of Ki-67 and isocitrate dehydrogenase-1 [IDH1]) [2]. In addition, several preoperative parameters, inflammatory markers and cancer-related biomarkers have been reported to prossess significance prognostic value [3,4]. Established biomarkers, such as IDH-1 mutation status, MGMT promoter methylation, and TERT promoter mutation, have improved prognostic models to some extent; however, considerable differences in results remain unexplained [5][6][7].

e role of inflammation in tumor progression and cancer treatment has led to extensive research on inflammatory markers like neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) in various malignancies [8]. In addition to inflammation, malnutrition is recognized as an important factor influencing treatment outcomes and survival in cancer patients [9]. Against this backdrop, the C-PLAN index has emerged as a comprehensive biomarker that integrates parameters reflecting inflammation, nutritional status and molecular pathway activity. It incorporates indicators such as performance status, C-reactive protein (CRP), albumin, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and NLR, and has been proposed as a potential tool for prognostic assessment in malignant tumors. e C-PLAN index has been only investigated in rare diseases, such as lung cancer [10], and metastatic renal cell carcinoma, because it is relatively new [11]. e C-PLAN index ranges from 0 to 5, with scores of 0-1 is defined as "good" and 2-5 defined as "poor" [12].

Given that HGGs are highly aggressive tumors associated with poor survival, there remains a need for reliable prognostic markers to predict outcomes and guide treatment and follow-up strategies. We believe that the C-PLAN index has not been adequately investigated for its predictive role in HGGs.

is study was conducted to evaluate the significance of the C-PLAN index in a cohort of patients with HGG and to determine its relationship with overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS).

div.head: Study design
div.p: is study was planned as a retrospective study and followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guideline [13].
e Helsinki Declaration or similar ethical standards were applied to all procedures and measurements in this study.
e Manisa Celal Bayar University Clinical Research Studies Ethical Board approved protocol number 20.478.486/3168.

div.head: Patients
div.p: is study retrospectively analyzed data from patients with high-grade glioma (HGG) who received radiotherapy/radiochemotherapy (radiotherapy combined with oral temozolomide) at the Department of Radiation Oncology xxx Hospital, between April 2011 and May 2024. e analysis was omitted data from 5 patients due to predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Inclusion criteria were: confirmed diagnosis of HGG, age over 18 years, and suitability for radiotherapy. Exclusion criteria were: incomplete patient data, presence of comorbidities, or multiple malignancies that may affect prognostic values. Data from 145 patients were initially collected. Due to incomplete or missing information, 5 cases were excluded from the final analysis. Data related to demographics (age, sex, body mass index [BMI], etc.), date of diagnosis, pre-radiotherapy blood test results, treatment timelines, pathological findings (e.g., IDH mutation status), recurrence data based on imaging, last follow-up date, and clinical details (surgical procedure, histological type and grade, radiotherapy dose) were extracted from patient medical records and electronic health records.

Performance status e general condition of patients was retrospectively evaluated using the Karnofsky Performance Status Scale (KPS) based on their medical records. e KPS is specifically designed to assess the physical and functional status of patients with chronic diseases [14]. e KPS score can range from zero to 100, with higher numbers indicating better overall health and vice versa [15]. OS was calculated from the date of first visit to the date of death or last fallow-up. PFS was defined as the time from the date of the first visit to the date of radiological or clinical disease progression (relapse).

div.head: Calculation of the C-PLAN index
div.p: e C-PLAN index was derived from five parameters, each scored as 0 or 1: C-reactive protein (CRP) < 1 mg/ dL, general condition score of 0-1, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) < 223 U/L, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte (NLR) < 3 and albumin > 3.5 g/dL. Each unfavorable parameter was scored 1, and each favorable parameter as 0.
e five component scores were summed to yield a total C-PLAN score, with scores of 0-1 was defined as "good", and 2-5 as "poor" [12].

div.head: Statistical analysis
div.p: Mean and standard deviation, as well as numbers and percentages, were employed to describe the data based on their classification, whether continuous or categorical. KS-SW normality tests, as well as skewness and kurtosis, along with graphical representation of the data, were used to analyze the normality. e Kaplan-Meier method was employed to analyze survival for dichotomous variables, including death as a cause for OS and PFS. e calculation of OS took into consideration the period from diagnosis to death or last follow-up. Univariate survival analysis was calculated by the log-rank test (Mantel-Cox) using the Kaplan-Meier method for dichotomous data.

Survival outcome was based on progression (relapse, re-admission) or death occurring during the follow-up period. e Cox multivariate regression analysis was performed by including variables that had a significant impact in univariate analysis, with a multicollinearity threshold r <.70 between independent variables. In multivariate analysis, the "Enter" strategy was followed. e data was analyzed via IBM SPSS v.27 (Chicago, IL, USA) at a 95% confidence interval, and the p-value of 0.05 was deemed to be significant.

div.head: Results
div.p: e screening and evaluation of 145 patients with HGG were conducted based on pre-defined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Due to missing data, five patients were not included in the analysis.

erefore, this study consisted of data from 140 HGG patients (83 men and 57 women). e mean follow-up time was 22.31 ± 28.97 months (median 12 months). Of the 140 patients, 122 (87.1%) died during follow-up. Six patients remained alive with the disease at the end of follow-up period, while 12 patients were disease-free. e mean age of patients was 56.61 ± 13.91 years, and the mean body mass index (BMI) was 26.85 ± 4.82 kg/ m 2 . At baseline, the majority of patients had a performance status score above 70 (n = 103, 73.6%). Of the 140 patients, 91 (65%) underwent complete resection, and 86.4% had a histopathological grade IV tumor. Histopathological examination showed that 110 patients (78.6%) were diagnosed with glioblastoma (GBM). In addition, 87.5% of the patients had IDH-negative status. Tumor localization was almost equally distributed between right (n = 73) and left (n = 67) cerebral hemispheres. Approximately one-quarter of the patients (n = 36, 25.7%) had tumors located in the parietal lobe, while headache (n = 43, 30.7%) was the most common initial symptom at diagnosis. Overall, 76.5% of patients experienced relapse. Among the patients included in this study, 74.3% (n = 104) had a C-PLAN index ≥ 2. e median C-PLAN index ranged from 2 to 3 (n = 46 and n = 37, respectively). Table 1 lists the demographic and clinical characteristics of the patients.

e median OS was 12 months (IQR 25-75: 7-21 months). According to the univariate analysis considering the dichotomous variables (Table 2), Neither the median OS (female: 11 months vs male: 14 months, p =.57) nor the PFS (female: 8 months vs male: 9 months, p =.76) had any statistically significant differences in gender. However, median OS and PFS were significantly affected by IDH status.

e median OS and PFS of patients with IDH-positive tumors were longer than those with IDHnegative tumors (80 months vs. 11 months, p < 0.001; 87.3 months vs. 25.8 months, p = 0.008, respectively). Our ) in the multivariate Cox regression analysis using the "Enter" method. However, the C-PLAN index was not significantly linked to OS ("good" vs. "poor", p = 0.176, HR = 0.69 [95% CI: 0.404, 1.18]). When PFS was analyzed, IDH status (p = 0.015, HR = 2.85 [95% CI: 1.22, 6.65]) and KPS score (p = 0.040, HR = 1.86 [95% CI: 1.02, 3.37]) had a significant impact on PFS, whereas the C-PLAN index (p = 0.09, HR = 0.606 [95% CI: 0.339, 1.08]) did not show a significant association.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: Our research indicates that this is the primary investigation to explore the potential impact of the C-PLAN index on the survival of patients with HGG receiving radiation therapy combined with oral temozolomide. Consistent with previous findings, this study identified performance status and IDH status as independent prognostic factors for HGG patient survival. Although the C-PLAN index showed significant prognostic value in univariate analysis, but it became insignificant after adjusting for confounding factors in multivariate analysis.

Aggressive tumors known as HGGs can resist systemic therapy and have poor prognosis. GBM, the most common subtype of HGG, is classified as grade IV by the World Health Organization (WHO) and is characterized by rapid progression and a extremely poor prognosis [16]. e median survival for patients with GBM has been reported to range from 12 to 15 months [17]. In the present study, the median OS was also 12 months, consistent with previous reports, which may be explained bt the fact that approximately 80% of our study cohort consisted of GBM patients. In contrast, Brown et al. [5] reported a median OS of 9.2 months. e range of OS values reported in the literature varies from 6 to 21.1 months, reflecting the heterogeneity of HGGs. Despite similar clinical and pathological features, patients exhibit distinct biological and clinical characteristics, underscoring the need for individualized treatment and prevention strategies [18]. Against this backdrop, current research has focused on various biomarkers, including IDH status, extent of surgical resection, tumor histopathological features, and patient performance status [2,3]. Consistent with previous reports, we also found that IDH status and performance status had significant predictive effects on OS and PFS. Several studies have demonstrated that highher KPS scores are associated with longer OS [19]. Incontrast, Almeida et al. [20] reported that performance status had no enermous impact on the survival of patients with GBM. However, their study primarily included elderly individuals (over 65 years of age), whereas in our cohort, the vast majority of patients (nearly 70%) were younger than 65 years. According to Gregucci et al. [21], KPS scores did not have a significant impact on survival rates for patients with GBM. In their study, the KPS threshold was set at 60, and the sample size was relatively small (n = 30). However, previous studies have shown that KPS scores below 70 are significantly associated with poorer prognosis [22]. erefore, in present study, the KPS threshold was set at 70. Similarly, Sasagasako et al. [23] reported that combining postoperative KPS scores with MRI images can improve AI-based predictive models, and they also used a KPS threshold of 70. In another study, Freeman et al. [15] reported that KPS scores were significant predictors in both univariate and multivariate analyses, however, their study concentrated on breast cancer patients with brain metastases.

e effects of gender on GBM are well documented in the literature. Male patients generally have a higher incidence of GBM and a poorer prognosis compared to female patients [24]. Yang et al. [25] suggested a potential physiological basis for this difference, reporting that male astrocytes may be more vulnerable to malignant transformation due to gender-specific, cell-intrinsic loss of TP53 function. In the present study, gender was not a significant factor affecting OS or PFS. In contrast, Katzendobler et al. [19] reported longer survival in female patients; however, this discrepancy may be attributable not only to their small sample size but also to the inclusion of patients with IDH wild-type tumors, as well as those astrocytomas and oligodendrogliomas.

With advances in the understanding of glioma biology, molecular profiling has become increasingly intergrated into clinical practice, enhancing prognostic accuracy and guiding personalized therapeutic strategies.

is paradigm shift toward precision oncology underscores the critical need for reliable biomarkers that enable refined patient stratification, tailored treatment approaches, and improved survival outcome in this complex disease [18]. In this context, the systemic immune-inflammation index (SII), examined using platelet, neutrophil and lymphocyte counts, has been recognized as a prognostic indicator in multiple malignancies and has recently been examined in several studies [26]. Pasqualetti F. et al. [27] demonstrated that neutrophil levels significantly influence OS. Previous studies have shown that high peripheral blood neutrophil counts are linked to treatment resistance and poor prognosis in patients with GBM. Furthermore, Topkan E. et al. [28] identified high pretreatment SII as an independent poor prognostic factor for both OS and PFS in a cohort of 167 GBM patients who underwent postoperative radiotherapy with concurrent oral temozolomide. Additionally, Zhang S. et al. [26], in their meta-analysis of eight studies comprising 1,426 glioma cases, reported that elevated SII values were associated with poorer OS and PFS, thereby influencing prognosis. More recently, in addition to SII, the C-PLAN index has been investigated in several cancers, including renal cell carcinoma [11], and has been identified as a valuable prognostic biomarker. As it incorporates indicators of inflammation, nutritional status, tumor burden/ metabolism, and functional status, the total score can be utilized to predict survival outcomes [10]. Furthermore, Sonehara et al. [12] reported that the C-PLAN index had significant predictive value in patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). As far as we know, there have been no studies that have examined the significance of the C-PLAN index in patients with HGG. In this study, univariate analysis revealed that the C-PLAN index was a significant predictor of OS and PFS. However, it did not retain statistical significance in the multivariate analysis. A few factors may explain this non-significant result. Because the C-PLAN index comprises five clinical parameters, patients with unfavorable scores in two of these parameters are categorized as "Poor" (score 2), the same classification assigned to those with all five parameters unfavorable ("Poor", score 5).

e complex and dynamic nature of HGGs may have influenced this scoring distribution. Nevertheless, this remains the first study to evaluate the potential prognostic impact of the C-PLAN index on survival in patients with HGG.

is study has both strengths and limitations that need to be acknowledged. e retrospective, single-center design and the fact that nearly all participants were White Caucasians may limit the generalizability of the findings. However, the nearly balanced gender distribution, relatively homogeneous sample (with most participants diagnosed with GBM), and sufficient sample size represent notable strengths of this study. Nevertheless, future multicenter, prospective studies with larger patient cohorts are warranted to provide stronger evidence.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: Multivariate analysis in this study revealed that IDH status and a KPS score greater than 70 were independent predictors of survival among patients with HGG. Although the C-PLAN index showed prognostic significant for OS and PFS in univariate analysis, it failed to maintain significance in multivariate analysis. To verify these findings, additional prospective multicenter studies are required.
